alt: Social identity at the centre of six groups it comes from: family, language, nationality, age group, faith and school. Definitions of inclusion, exclusion and belonging, and two contested ideas: integration, where groups mix and share institutions, and multiculturalism, where groups keep distinct identities within one society.
caption: Identity comes from the groups we belong to; inclusion decides whether we can take part.

after: ## Finding issues at global, national and local level
alt: A test of whether a statement is an issue: “Discrimination is bad” is not, because almost nobody disagrees; whether school dress rules should allow cultural exceptions is, because people answer differently. A table gives an issue at each level: global accessibility agreements, national quotas, and local wheelchair access.
caption: A good issue divides opinion.

after: ## Perspectives: who sees the issue differently, and why
alt: Four perspectives on school dress rules: some parents and teachers want one uniform to reduce visible wealth differences; a government wants clear national rules; other families want room for cultural dress and hairstyles; students see appearance as self-expression and may feel excluded. Global non-discrimination principles do not settle the detail.
caption: Each perspective rests on a value: fairness, clarity, heritage or self-expression.

alt: Six causes of exclusion (physical barriers, cost, language differences, stereotypes, rules designed for the majority, lack of information) lead to consequences for individuals (loneliness, missed education or jobs), communities (less trust, wasted talent) and countries (lower output and tension, or where inclusion succeeds, wider skills and ideas).
caption: Name who is affected by exclusion and how.

alt: Sixty dots, 21 highlighted, show that 21 of 60 older residents surveyed by a fictional Kelton community centre (35%) had no one to talk to most weeks. People who never visit the centre were probably missed, so the real figure could be higher. A cause chain: evening buses stop, residents stop going to events, and they have fewer chances to meet people.
caption: Ask who a survey missed: here, the most isolated people.

alt: A table evaluates four reference points: UDHR Article 2, the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, SDG target 10.2, and the WHO estimate that about 1.3 billion people, 1 in 6, have significant disability. Each has a strength and limitation. Using a global figure to justify a local decision is a jump in reasoning.
caption: A credible source can still be used in weak reasoning.

alt: A student-run culture club is assessed: it targets the cause by helping newcomers meet others and valuing their background, at low cost, but depends on committed leaders, may attract confident students and does not reach those who never attend. It works best alongside other actions. Six questions for judging any action follow.
caption: A cheap, targeted action can still need others alongside it.
